outputs.L1:
**How Do I Love Thee? Let Me Count the Ways**

How do I love thee? Let me count the ways.  
I love thee to the depth and breadth and height  
My soul can reach, when feeling out of sight  
For the ends of being and ideal grace.  
I love thee to the level of every day’s  
Most quiet need, by sun and candle-light.  
I love thee freely, as men strive for right;  
I love thee purely, as they turn from praise.  
I love thee with the passion put to use  
In my old griefs, and with my childhood’s faith.  
I love thee with a love I seemed to lose  
With my lost saints. I love thee with the breath,  
Smiles, tears, of all my life; and, if God choose,  
I shall but love thee better after death.

**Poetry Out Loud Note:** In the print anthology, this poem is titled simply *“How do I love thee? Let me count the ways.”* The student may use either title during their recitation.
outputs.L2:
In what ways do I love you? I will try to name them.  
My love reaches as far as my soul can extend—  
to every depth, width, and height it can imagine  
while searching beyond the visible world  
toward existence’s limits and perfect grace.  

I love you in the measure of life’s ordinary, quiet necessities,  
in daylight and by candlelight.  
I love you willingly, like those who struggle for justice;  
I love you sincerely, like those who refuse empty praise.  

I love you with the intensity once spent on my former sorrows,  
and with the trusting belief I had as a child.  
I love you with the devotion I thought I had lost  
when I lost the holy figures I once cherished.  

I love you with every breath, every smile, and every tear  
of my whole life; and if God allows it,  
I will love you even more after death.  

Poetry Out Loud note: In the printed anthology, the poem is listed under the title “How do I love thee? Let me count the ways.” A student reciting it may use either title.
outputs.L3:
The speaker describes a love that is vast, profound, and deeply spiritual. It reaches to the fullest depth, breadth, and height of the soul, suggesting a feeling that cannot be measured by ordinary limits. This love is not shallow or temporary; it fills the speaker’s entire being and extends as far as the soul itself can reach.

At the same time, the speaker’s love is present in the simple realities of everyday life. It exists in ordinary moments, in quiet routines, and in the small needs that shape daily living. This makes the love feel both grand and intimate: it is not only an elevated emotional or spiritual experience, but also something lived out through constant care, attention, and devotion.

The speaker also presents this love as free, pure, and passionate. It is given willingly, without force or expectation, and it carries a moral sincerity that makes it feel noble and true. The love is connected to intense feeling, but also to the speaker’s past experiences, including grief and the innocent faith of childhood. In this way, the love gathers together different parts of the speaker’s life—joy, sorrow, memory, belief, and desire.

The speaker loves with every part of existence, including breath, smiles, and tears. Love is shown not merely as an emotion, but as something woven into the body, the spirit, and the whole pattern of life. Every sign of living becomes a way of loving: each breath, each moment of happiness, and each sorrow contributes to the speaker’s devotion.

Finally, the speaker believes that such love may not end with death. Instead, it may continue beyond earthly life and even grow stronger in the afterlife. This gives the love an eternal quality, suggesting that it belongs not only to the present world but also to a spiritual realm beyond it. Overall, the speaker portrays love as total, enduring, and sacred—an affection that embraces all of life and reaches beyond death itself.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents romantic love as something too vast to be measured in ordinary terms, yet the speaker tries to “count” or describe it by naming the many ways it fills her life. Love is shown not merely as a feeling, but as a force that reaches the highest levels of the soul. The speaker loves with a depth and height that suggest spiritual expansion, as though love connects her to something beyond the physical world. This gives the poem a sense of reverence, making romantic love appear sacred rather than purely emotional.

At the same time, the poem grounds love in everyday devotion. The speaker loves freely and constantly, in the quiet moments of daily life as well as in its most intense experiences. Her love is compared to moral purity, suggesting that it is sincere, unselfish, and guided by truth rather than desire or obligation. She also connects her present love to her past, saying that it contains the passion once spent on old griefs and the innocent faith she had as a child. In this way, love gathers together all parts of her life—her sorrow, hope, memory, belief, and personal growth.

By the end of the poem, love is presented as complete and enduring. The speaker loves with her whole being: her breath, smiles, tears, and entire existence are involved in it. The poem’s significance lies in its portrayal of true love as boundless, spiritual, and lasting. It goes beyond ordinary human experience because it is not limited to time, physical presence, or even death. The final suggestion that love may continue “after death” gives the poem its deepest power, presenting love as eternal and capable of surviving beyond mortal life.

**How, Let, For**

How do we begin something new? Often, the first step is simply deciding to try. Whether it is learning a skill, starting a project, or changing a habit, progress begins with curiosity and courage.

Let yourself make mistakes along the way. Mistakes are not signs of failure; they are part of learning. When you allow yourself to grow slowly, you become more confident and patient.

For every challenge, there is an opportunity to improve. For every question, there is a chance to discover something useful. By asking how, letting yourself learn, and working for a purpose, you can move forward with strength and hope.

## “How Do I Love Thee?” by Elizabeth Barrett Browning

How do I love thee? Let me count the ways.  
I love thee to the depth and breadth and height  
My soul can reach, when feeling out of sight  
For the ends of being and ideal grace.  
I love thee to the level of every day’s  
Most quiet need, by sun and candle-light.  
I love thee freely, as men strive for right.  
I love thee purely, as they turn from praise.  
I love thee with the passion put to use  
In my old griefs, and with my childhood’s faith.  
I love thee with a love I seemed to lose  
With my lost saints. I love thee with the breath,  
Smiles, tears, of all my life; and, if God choose,  
I shall but love thee better after death.
